Q7.paragraph: **The Quran condemns apostasy severely but names no worldly punishment for it.** Verse 2:217 warns that whoever "reverts from his religion [to disbelief] and dies while he is a disbeliever – for those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter". Alalwani surveyed every Quranic use of *ridda* and concludes that "None of the verses… makes any mention of an earthly punishment for the sin or crime of apostasy" (ch. 2). In the foreword to the abridged edition he adds that the Quran "refers to individuals repeatedly returning to unbelief after having believed, but does not mention that they should be killed or punished." Reformists also rely on 2:256: "There shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion."

**Limit:** Jurists held that the Sunna can add rulings the Quran does not state. Alalwani records that al-Shafiʿi "approached the issue of apostasy in light of" four verses, 8:39, 9:5, 2:217 and 39:65, in support of the death penalty.

**Two authentic hadith carry the legal weight.** The first is narrated by ʿIkrima. ʿAli had burnt some people, and Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Had I been in his place I would not have burnt them… No doubt, I would have killed them, for the Prophet said, 'If somebody (a Muslim) discards his religion, kill him'" ({hadith:bukhari:3017}; parallel {hadith:bukhari:6922}, where the people are called *zanādiqa*, hidden heretics). Both are sahih by inclusion in al-Bukhari. In Arabic the third case joins two phrases. Al-Bukhari's wording is *al-māriq min al-dīn al-tārik al-jamāʿa*, "the one who goes out of the religion, leaving the community"; Muslim's is *al-tārik li-dīnihi al-mufāriq li-l-jamāʿa*, "the deserter of his religion, abandoning the community". In Arabic the third case is *al-tārik li-l-jamāʿa*, "abandoning the community".

**Did the Prophet (pbuh) ever execute anyone only for leaving Islam?** Alalwani: "never in his entire life did the Prophet put an apostate to death". He argues that reported killings were "due to the individuals' participation in war crimes or murder, not due to their apostasy" (ch. 3). The men of ʿUkl (in some reports ʿUrayna) both left Islam and killed a herdsman and drove off the camels (Bukhari 6802, from Anas). Alalwani reads such cases as punishment for the crimes; the hadith itself names both the apostasy and the killing, so the case cannot settle the question either way. Two further points support this. Many people who left after the Night Journey were not harmed. And the Treaty of Hudaybiyya let anyone who left the Muslim camp return to Quraysh "freely without reprisal".

**Limit:** This is partly an argument from silence, and it does not remove the general wording. At the conquest of Mecca, the Prophet (pbuh) ordered Ibn Khatal killed even as he clung to the Kaʿba's curtains ({hadith:abudawud:2685}); the hadith gives no reason, and the commentators explain that he had murdered the Muslim companion travelling with him. ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Sarh, who had also left Islam, was spared: ʿUthman interceded, and the Prophet (pbuh), after hesitating, accepted his pledge ({hadith:abudawud:4359}). The two cases are used on both sides of the modern debate: one ends in execution, apparently for murder; the other in pardon.

Q7.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
Q7.paragraph: **Who questioned execution early?** Alalwani names ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, a Companion, and two later scholars, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi and Sufyan al-Thawri, whose views, he says, "did not receive publicity or wide circulation" (ch. 1). The usual basis for ʿUmar is the *Muwatta* report (no. 1420). and said, "I am not pleased since it has come to me!" (*Muwatta* 1420; graded *ḥasan* by al-Albani). Al-Qaradawi reports ʿUmar's view as asking the apostate to repent for as long as he lives, imprisoned and fed (IslamOnline, "al-Ridda wa-ʿuqubat al-murtadd"). Ibn Qudama in fact lists al-Nakhaʿi among those who made no distinction between male and female apostates in the death penalty (*al-Mughni* 12/264). The dissents are thinly documented.

Q7.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
Q7.paragraph:
**Who holds the "not for belief alone" view today?**
- **Taha Jabir Alalwani** Taha Jabir al-Alwani (1935–2016) wrote that as long as apostasy "has not been accompanied by anything else that would be deemed a criminal act… it remains strictly between God and the individual, and is not the province of earthly rulers" (*Apostasy in Islam*, 2011, p. 41).
- **Ali Gomaa** (Grand Mufti of Egypt 2003–2013). Egypt's Dar al-Iftaʾ, under Ali Gomaa, answered the question "Can a person who is a Muslim choose a religion other than Islam?": "If the case in question is one of merely rejecting faith, then there is no worldly punishment"; the state steps in only when "the crime of undermining the foundations of the society is added to the sin of apostasy" (fatwa 8002). Gulf News (Ramadan Al Sherbini, 25 July 2007) then quoted him: "What I actually said is that Islam prohibits a Muslim from changing his religion and that apostasy is a crime, which must be punished." His position is real, but its wording is disputed.
- **Mohammad Hashim Kamali and Tariq Ramadan**: reported, with Alalwani, as holding that "the Qur'an does not prescribe a temporal punishment for apostasy" (secondary source).
- **Abdullah and Hassan Saeed**: argue similarly (secondary summary only).

Q7.section: fiqh — What the four schools hold
Q7.paragraph:
**All four schools prescribe death for the unrepentant adult male apostate. They differ on the waiting period and on women.** The waiting period is *istitāba*, the formal invitation to repent.
- **Hanafi:** al-Kasani (*Badaʾiʿ* 7/134) says asking him to repent is "recommended… but it is not obligatory". Al-Sarakhsi (as quoted) grants three days if the apostate asks. On women, Ibn Qudama reports Abu Hanifa's view that a female apostate "is compelled to Islam by imprisonment and beating, and is not killed" (*al-Mughni* 12/265).
- **Maliki:** Khalil's *Mukhtasar*: "He is asked to repent for three days, without hunger, thirst or punishment; if he repents [he is left], otherwise he is killed." Women are treated like men.
- **Shafi'i:** al-Nawawi (*Minhaj* p. 293): asking the male and female apostate to repent is obligatory (one view: recommended) and immediate (one view: three days); "if they persist, they are killed."
- **Hanbali:** Ibn Qudama (*al-Mughni* 1538) quotes al-Khiraqi: "Whoever apostatises from Islam, man or woman, being adult and sane, is invited back for three days… otherwise he is killed." He adds a second narration from Ahmad that the invitation is only recommended.

Q7.section: objection — The strongest objections, and the replies
Q7.paragraph: **"Will God punish me for doubting?"** *Reply:* Doubt is not disbelief. In Alalwani's reading, apostasy affects faith only when one "open[s] his or her heart consciously and willingly to a denial of the truth". *Istitāba* existed to answer doubts: al-Shirbini notes that the apostate "may have been struck by a doubt". When Companions told the Prophet (pbuh) that they found thoughts in their minds too grave to speak of, he said: "That is the faith manifest" ({hadith:muslim:132}).

Q13.paragraph: **The Quran says the people of the Fire abide "therein forever" (*khālidīna fīhā abadan*) at 4:169, 33:65 and 72:23. In Sura Hud it attaches an exception.** Verse 11:107: "[They will be] abiding therein as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except what your Lord should will. Indeed, your Lord is an effecter of what He intends." They also cited 78:23's *aḥqāb* ("ages") as a long but countable period; Saheeh International adds "[unending]", following the majority reading.

Q13.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
Q13.paragraph: **Ibn Taymiyya did not merely say "there is no consensus"; he argued that the punishment ends.** According to Jon Hoover, *Fanāʾ al-nār* was Ibn Taymiyya's last work, written "in response to an inquiry from Ibn al-Qayyim about the duration of punishment and the Fire". It rejects Jahm ibn Safwan's view that both abodes perish. Hoover summarises its conclusion: "the reward of Paradise is everlasting while the chastisement of unbelievers in Hell-Fire will end". He adds that Ibn Taymiyya's reasoning "leads to the conclusion that God will use Hell-fire to bring all creatures into complete accord with the purposes for which they were naturally constituted". In Hoover's words, for both men "Hell is therapeutic and reformative." The treatise cites Companion reports, among them from ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas (Hoover, 2015). It takes *fanāʾ* to mean that the punishment ceases, not necessarily that the Fire ceases to exist. Hoover has also documented later attempts to deny the treatise or play it down: al-Albani's claim that it was written "before mastering the religious sciences", and ʿAli al-Harbi's 1990 book (Hoover, in *Debating Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Qayyim*, de Gruyter 2013, 377–399).

Q13.section: objection — The strongest objections, and the replies
Q13.paragraph: **"Fear of Hell harms people."** *Reply:* For some people it does. Clinicians call this scrupulosity, a religious form of OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder), known among Muslims as *waswās*. One of five participants in a small UK interview study said: "Then I thought to myself - 'Oh no, I'm going to Hell'. Like, I was just constantly thinking to myself about Hell fire" (Hamlaoui et al., *JBIMA*).

The justice of eternal Hell cannot be demonstrated to someone outside faith. Ibn Kathir reads the exception in 11:107 ("except what your Lord should will") as referring to "the disobedient among the people of Tawhid", believers who sinned and will be brought out of the Fire by intercession; those who remain after that, he says, remain forever. He takes "as long as the heavens and the earth endure" as an Arab way of saying "forever", following al-Tabari.

Q14.paragraph: **The Quran contains both a broad promise and an exclusive claim.** Verse 2:62 (cf. 5:69): "Indeed, those who believed and those who were Jews or Christians or Sabeans [before Prophet Muhammad] - those [among them] who believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteousness - will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve." Verse 3:85: "And whoever desires other than Islam as religion – never will it be accepted from him, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers." Verse 17:15 states the governing principle: "And never would We punish until We sent a messenger."

**What does "Islam" mean in 3:85?** Ibn Kathir uses both senses. Ibn Kathir describes Islam as "the religion that He sent His Books and Messengers with, which is the worship of Allah Alone without partners", and, on 2:62, says that after Muhammad (pbuh) was sent, God accepts no deed "unless it conforms to the Law of Muhammad".

**The testing of the people of *fatra*.** *Fatra* means an interval between prophets. They are commanded to enter the fire: "if they enter Hell, it will become cool and safe for them" (Musnad Ahmad 16301, tohed.com translation). The parallel from Abu Hurayra adds: "whoever does not enter it will be dragged to it."

Q31.paragraph: **Praying for guidance.** When the tribe of Daws refused Islam, the Prophet (pbuh) prayed: "O Allah! Give guidance to the Daus (tribe) and bring them (to Islam)!" ({hadith:bukhari:4392}).

**How scholars read Muslim 203 and 976.** Mulla ʿAli al-Qari and Ibrahim al-Halabi read them literally. Al-Suyuti argued: "The Prophet's parents died before he was sent as Prophet and there is no punishment for them, since (We never punish until We send a messenger (whom they reject)) (17:15). Our Ash'ari Imams among those in kalam, usul, and fiqh agree on the statement that one who dies while da'wa has not reached him, dies saved" (trans. Haddad). (The bracket "(whom they reject)" is the translator's.) Our Ashʿari Imams… agree… that one who dies while daʿwa has not reached him, dies saved." **Limit:** his view requires setting aside the plain sense of two sahih hadiths. Many scholars rejected it, and some reports he used are judged fabricated.

Q31.section: fiqh — What the four schools hold
Q31.paragraph:
- **Forgiveness for a deceased non-Muslim** is forbidden (9:113; Muslim 976). Islamweb: "it is not permissible to supplicate for him or seek forgiveness for him."
- **Prayer for a living relative's guidance** is permitted, following the Daws precedent.
- **Shafiʿi:** al-Nawawi: "It is permissible for a Muslim to follow the funeral procession of a non-Muslim relative" (*Minhāj*, p. 62); visiting the grave is permitted according to the chosen opinion of the majority (*al-Majmūʿ* 5/144), both as given by the Federal Territory Mufti of Malaysia. He also reports that visiting the grave is allowed according to the majority (*al-Majmuʿ* 5/144).
- **Maliki:** Malik held that a Muslim should not wash his father who died a disbeliever, "nor should he follow the funeral procession, nor should he go to his funeral" (*al-Mudawwana* 1/261, as quoted by the Federal Territory Mufti). (Any exception for burial needs its own source.)
- **Hanbali:** asked about a non-Muslim parent or close relative, Ahmad said: "If this non-Muslim is a father, mother, brother, or a close relative, and he attended it, then there is no harm in that." He cited ʿUmar's instruction to Abu Waʾil about his Christian mother: "Ride in her funeral procession and be in front of her" (Ibn al-Qayyim, *Aḥkām Ahl al-Dhimma*, via Islamweb 367663).
- **Hanafi:** condolence to a non-Muslim is allowed, with a formula of comfort (*al-Fatawa al-Hindiyya* 5/348).
- **Visiting the grave and grieving** are permitted on the basis of Muslim 976.
- **A minority position:** some modern Hanafi (Deobandi) fatwas forbid attending a non-Muslim's funeral. "It is not permissible" (Mufti Zakaria Makada, Muftionline, citing *al-Durr al-Mukhtār* 2/230). Faraz Rabbani, also Hanafi, answers: "Yes, it is permitted to attend the funeral of a non-Muslim parent, relative, neighbor, or associate", citing *al-Baḥr al-Rāʾiq* 2/205: "one may follow their funeral from afar".

Q29.paragraph: **The "hidden treasure" saying is not a hadith.** Many people quote: "I was a hidden treasure; I loved to be known. Hence I created the world so that I would be known" (one of several English versions given by *Wikipedia*). It has no chain of narrators. According to al-ʿAjluni's *Kashf al-Khafaʾ*, Ibn Taymiyya said that "it was not said by the Prophet (peace be upon him)" and that it has "neither Sahih (authentic) nor Daʿif (weak) Sanad (chain of narrators)", and that al-Zarkashi, Ibn Hajar, al-Suyuti and others agreed (as reported by *al-Feqh* and by Islamweb, fatwa 14995). The Hadith Answers team calls it "a fabrication" and says one "should therefore abstain from quoting it", citing *al-Maqasid al-Hasana* (no. 838) and other works. It is popular because it puts into one sentence an idea many Sufis hold: that God created so that He would be known and loved (*Wikipedia*). Its meaning may be defended on other grounds, but it must not be presented as the Prophet's (pbuh) words.

Q33.paragraph: **It records demands for miracles, and refuses them.** In Sura al-Isra (Meccan), the Prophet's (pbuh) opponents say: "We will not believe you until you break open for us from the ground a spring. / Or [until] you have a garden of palm tress and grapes and make rivers gush forth within them in force [and abundance] / Or you make the heaven fall upon us in fragments as you have claimed or you bring Allah and the angels before [us] / Or you have a house of gold or you ascend into the sky. And [even then], we will not believe in your ascension…" (17:90–93). To the demands for a spring, a garden, a house of gold and a ladder to the sky (17:90–93), the reply the Prophet (pbuh) is told to give is: "Exalted is my Lord! Was I ever but a human messenger?" (17:93).

Q20.paragraph: **The revisionist chronologies.** An anonymous contributor to the Yaqeen Institute (2018) replies that… [as now], and that at Uhud Aisha was carrying water, "acting as a nurse, not as a combatant". Kandhlawi's book itself has not yet been consulted.

Q20.section: science — What the evidence on harm shows
Q20.paragraph: **What Muslim-majority states do now.** According to Musawah, Egypt and Kuwait set 18 for both sexes and bar registering younger marriages; Pakistan's Sindh province criminalises marriage under 18; Jordan sets 18 with a judicial exception down to 15 (Musawah's page also lists Iraq this way. In 2025 Iraq amended its personal status law so that couples may choose to be governed by a Shiʿi (Jaʿfari) code instead of the 1959 law; human rights groups fear it will allow lower marriage ages, but when Human Rights Watch reported in March 2025 the code had not yet been written, and the 1959 law sets 18, or 15 with a judge's permission); Morocco, Tunisia, Oman and the UAE set 18 with judicial exceptions; Algeria sets 19; Indonesia sets 19 but allows court exceptions with no floor. So the law varies, and exceptions remain a real problem.

Q21.paragraph: **The Ottoman steps.** The public slave market in Istanbul was closed in 1846–47, but the trade went on in private, reportedly even among the highest officials (Karamursel, *IJMES*, 2025). A ban on the Circassian and Georgian slave trade in 1854 contributed to a rebellion in the Hijaz, which led to the Hijaz being exempted (Miers, cited by *Wikipedia*). The firman of 1857 "formally prohibited the import of African slaves" but "did not prohibit slavery as such", excluded the Hijaz, and "was never enforced in practice". The Kanunname of 1889 formally banned the trade.

**The twentieth century.** Saudi Arabia formally abolished slavery in 1962: a June 1962 royal decree banned the sale and purchase of people, and in November 1962 King Faisal prohibited owning slaves (Miers, cited by *Wikipedia*). Mauritania abolished slavery in 1981 but made it a crime only in 2007; at that time Anti-Slavery International reported that "Thousands of people in Mauritania are enslaved as a result of being born into an established slave class."

**Did Islam produce an abolitionist movement?** Kecia Ali (cited by *Wikipedia*) writes that "there has not been a strong internally developed critique of past or present slaveholding practices". Brown's book contrasts the Euro-American tradition, where abolitionism arose, with others, including Islam, which "did not consensually abolish slavery" (Azzuhri). But there were Muslim abolitionist arguments: Tunisian reformers argued for abolition "on the basis of Islamic law", and Ameer Ali argued that "the Qur'an disapproved of slavery, but Muhammad could not abolish the institution overnight" (Wikipedia). In the late Ottoman Empire, the writer Ahmed Midhat "saw slavery as an incorrigible wrong that was best abolished altogether", and Sezai's novel *Sergüzeşt* attacked the trade (Karamursel, *IJMES*, 2025). These were writers, not jurists, and they did not end slavery.

Q21.section: reasoning — The argument for prohibition today
Q21.paragraph: **Brown's view.** As Aammari summarises it, Brown holds that "God wishes freedom" (p. 264), so abolition is the best way to realise that wish, and that modern norms of consent make concubinage a "dead letter" in Islamic law and ethics. The Iranian scholar Mohsen Kadivar argues that slavery is now "forbidden and illegitimate", because "the reasonable people consider it to be detested and oppressive". He treats its earlier permission as a temporary ruling "whose era has passed", and says explicitly that this is not "technical abrogation" ("The Issue of Slavery in Contemporary Islam", 2018).

- **Classical law** — slavery and concubinage permitted, with rights and paths to freedom; consent to sex not required (Kecia Ali, 2017).
- **Ibn ʿAshur** — the Sharia aims at freedom and reduced slavery's causes.
- **Brown (2019)** — abolition not indigenous to Islam, but consistent with God's wish for freedom; concubinage a "dead letter" today.
- **Kecia Ali** — the tradition must face the absence of consent.
- **The Open Letter (2014)** — reintroducing slavery is forbidden by consensus.
- **Kadivar** — slavery is now "forbidden and illegitimate"; its earlier permission was temporary, "whose era has passed", not abrogated (2018).
- **Mawdudi** (as criticised by Clarence-Smith) — refused to give up slavery in principle.

Q22.paragraph: **9:29 in its setting.** "Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day and who do not consider unlawful what Allah and His Messenger have made unlawful and who do not adopt the religion of truth from those who were given the Scripture - [fight] until they give the jizyah willingly while they are humbled" (9:29). Ibn Kathir connects it with the campaign of Tabuk, when the Prophet (pbuh) marched "towards Ash-Sham to fight the Romans". Al-Shafiʿi, as quoted by al-Qaradawi, explained "while they are humbled" as meaning "they should submit to the Islamic judgment regarding them" (*Fiqh al-Jihad* 2/797).

**What Qurayza did.** Lecker writes that Qurayza "probably remained neutral": they lent the Muslims tools for digging the trench but also sold provisions to the besiegers. Ibn Kathir reports that Huyayy ibn Akhtab, leader of al-Nadir, persuaded Qurayza's leader Kaʿb ibn Asad to break their covenant, promising to join them in their fortress if the coalition left. So the "breach" was, at the least, negotiating with an army besieging the city they were bound not to fight against; how far it went is disputed.

**The siege and the verdict.** After the coalition withdrew, the Muslims besieged Qurayza for twenty-five days (Ibn Kathir on 33:26). They surrendered unconditionally, and their fate was "reportedly decided not by Muhammad" but by Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, the gravely wounded leader of the Aws, Qurayza's former allies; some of the Aws opposed his decision (Lecker). One woman was also executed. ʿAʾisha (ra), who saw her before her death, says only that she was killed for "a new act" she had committed ({hadith:abudawud:2671}; al-Albani: *ḥasan*). Ibn Hisham (d. 833) adds that she was the one who threw a millstone on Khallad ibn Suwayd and killed him; the commentator al-Khattabi, as cited in *ʿAwn al-Maʿbūd*, says instead that she had insulted the Prophet (pbuh).

**The numbers.** The hadith collections give no number. Ibn Ishaq, in Ibn Hisham's edition, says: "They were six hundred or seven hundred; the one who gives the highest number says between eight hundred and nine hundred" — with no chain of transmitters for the figure. Ibn Kathir, on 33:26, gives "between seven hundred and eight hundred". The hadith collections give no number. Kister estimated the women and children at about 1,000. Kirazli (2019) argues that "the number of Jews punished in this incident were significantly less than what is reported by Ibn Isḥāq".

The early sources disagree on the number executed: al-Tabari reports "600 or 700", with the largest estimate "between 800 and 900"; Ibn Kathir, on 33:26, "between seven hundred and eight hundred"; the hadith collections give no number (as summarised in *Wikipedia*, "Siege of Banu Qurayza"; the primary texts have not yet been consulted).

Q22.section: scholars — How scholars have read 9:5 and 9:29
Q22.paragraph: **Modern readings.** Muhammad Abdel Haleem says the targeted polytheists "continuously broke their agreements and aided others against the Muslims", that the passage exempts those who kept their treaties (9:4, 9:7), and that 9:6 "orders that those enemies seeking safe-conduct should be protected"; he rejects the humiliation reading of 9:29. Patricia Crone, a non-Muslim historian, says 9:5 "is directed against a particular group accused of oath-breaking and aggression" (Wikipedia, "Sword Verse"). The Ottoman Empire abolished the jizya with the reform decree of 1856 (*Hatt-ı Hümâyun*); a tax for exemption from military service took its place (Thompson, *Encyclopedia of the Modern Middle East*). The 2014 Open Letter to al-Baghdadi states: "Jihad in Islam is defensive war."

Q25.section: fiqh — What the four schools hold
Q25.paragraph: **Desire and act.** El-Rouayheb argues that the Arab-Islamic world of 1500–1800 "lacked the concept of homosexuality": it judged acts and roles, and its sources include a large body of Arabic love poetry. The modern idea of a fixed "orientation" did not exist; the law judged acts.

Q6.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
Q6.paragraph:
**What classical scholars said about "strike".** Ayesha Chaudhry's study of pre-colonial exegesis and law concludes that pre-modern scholars "unanimously interpreted *wadribuhunna* as hitting, striking or beating" and disagreed only on "the procedure and the extent" (Mariam Noor, review in *LUMS Law Journal* 3:1, 2016, pp. 110–118). The range of what was allowed ran "from hitting with a handkerchief to lashing the wife hundred or more times with a whip" (same review). Within that, they set limits:
- Ibn ʿAbbas (ra), asked what "without severity" means, said: "the siwak (tooth-stick) and the like" (via al-Tabari, as reported by *Wikipedia*). Ibn Kathir reports that "Ibn 'Abbas and several others said that the Ayah refers to a beating that is not violent", and al-Hasan al-Basri "a beating that is not severe". The Prophet (pbuh), asked about a wife's rights, said: "do not strike her on the face, do not revile her or separate yourself from her except in the house" ({hadith:abudawud:2142}; al-Albani: *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*).
- **Shafiʿi school:** al-Shafiʿi held that "hitting is permitted, but not hitting is preferable" (as reported by *Wikipedia*); the school classed it as discouraged (*makrūh*) (Chaudhry, per the review).
- **Hanafi:** al-Jassas required "a non-violent blow with siwak" or similar (Wikipedia); the school gave the husband disciplinary power "with minimal legal accountability" (Chaudhry, per the review).
- **Maliki:** made the husband liable for compensation if discipline caused harm (Chaudhry, per the review).
- **ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah**, a leading Meccan scholar, advised a husband not to beat his wife even if she ignored him, and to express his anger another way (Jonathan Brown, as reported by *Wikipedia*).
Chaudhry's summary of the pre-colonial tradition: "None of them believed it to be unacceptable or forbidden for husbands to hit their wives" (review).

Q6.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
Q6.paragraph: **Modern readings.** Chaudhry identifies four strategies: traditionalists who keep the permission as a last resort; neo-traditionalists for whom "the hitting is meant to be symbolic rather than punitive"; progressives who hold "there is no room for husbands to hit their wives"; and reformists who read the word as "separation" (review). Laleh Bakhtiar's translation, *The Sublime Quran* (2007), renders the verb "go away from them".

Q6.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
Q6.paragraph: **Testimony.** Ibn Rushd reports general agreement on 2:282 in financial matters. Abu Hanifa accepted women's testimony in matters such as marriage and divorce; Malik did not; most scholars accepted women's testimony alone in matters men rarely witness, such as childbirth (Wikipedia, "Status of women's testimony"). Ibn al-Qayyim (d. 1350) wrote that "the woman is equal to the man in truthfulness, honesty, and piety", and that a second woman is added only where forgetting is feared (*al-Ṭuruq al-Ḥukmiyya* 1/136, trans. Abu Amina Elias). Taha Jabir al-ʿAlwani (1996) argues that the verse's instructions were "recommended or merely instructional (*irshad*) and without legal import", and that such transactions "were not often matters of" women's concern under "the prevailing social conditions" (abstract).

Q23.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
Q23.paragraph: **The common reading.** On a widely held reading, the justice required in 4:3 is justice in what a man can control — maintenance, housing, time — and 4:129 is about feelings, which he cannot fully control; then the two verses do not cancel each other. Saheeh's bracket "[in feeling]" reflects this reading. Ibn Kathir, reporting Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿUbayda al-Salmani, Mujahid, al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Dahhak, explains that even when a husband divides his nights justly, "there will still be various degrees concerning love, desire and sexual intimacy" — that is the equality 4:129 says cannot be reached. What can be controlled — time and maintenance — must be equal, and he must not "incline completely" and leave a wife "hanging" (4:129). The Prophet (pbuh) used to pray: "O Allah! This is my division in what I own, so do not blame me for what You own and I do not own", meaning the heart (reported by Abu Dawud; Ibn Kathir: chain *ṣaḥīḥ*).

Q23.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
Q23.paragraph: **ʿAbduh and Riḍā.** Muhammad ʿAbduh (d. 1905) "concluded that polygamy is an injustice to both women and children" and "should only be permissible in cases of necessity" (Rasha Dewedar, Musawah, 2021). The source does not say in which work, and *Tafsir al-Manar* itself has not been read. Their reading takes 4:3 and 4:129 together as showing that the condition is rarely met. *Tafsir al-Manar* itself has not yet been consulted.

**Legal bans and restrictions.** Türkiye's Civil Code of 1926 (in force 4 October 1926) adopted monogamy (Doyran, 2023). Tunisia's 1956 Code of Personal Status made polygyny an offence "liable for a prison sentence of one year and/or a fine" (Emory Law, "Islamic Family Law: Tunisia"); President Bourguiba argued that equal treatment could not be assured, and the Tunisian scholar Muhammad al-Fadil ibn ʿAshur later supported the Code as a possible interpretation of Islam (Wikipedia, citing Perkins). In Pakistan, a man needs written permission from an Arbitration Council, which must find the new marriage "necessary, and just"; his application must say whether his wife consents (Muslim Family Laws Ordinance 1961). Iran's pre-1979 law required court permission and the first wife's consent; that law was repealed after the revolution, and the present rules were not checked.

Q24.paragraph: The four Sunni schools hold that a free woman must cover all her body except her face and hands before men outside her close family, which includes the hair. They base this on 24:31, which tells believing women to draw their *khimār* — a word that in Arabic meant a head covering — over their chests, on 33:59, and on the hadith. A modern minority (for example Muhammad Shahrur) disagrees. Whether to wear it is a question of conscience before God; who may enforce it is a separate question. The Quran says "there shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion" (2:256); Egypt's Dar al-Iftaʾ (fatwa 7272, 2014) says a father must advise but must not force, beat or harm his daughter, because "any compulsion will lead her to be hypocritical". Bans harm women too: France's 2004 school ban reduced Muslim girls' secondary education. This site's firm line is against coercion in either direction.

**2. Who may enforce it, and how?** Ibn ʿAbbas reports that before Islam some women of Medina whose children did not survive vowed to raise a child as a Jew; when the Banu Nadir were expelled, some children of the Ansar were among them, and their families wanted to keep them back — and 2:256 was revealed: "There shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion" ({hadith:abudawud:2682}; al-Albani: *ṣaḥīḥ*). Its direct subject is conversion. Ibn Taymiyya is quoted as saying "Most of the salaf" considered it "neither specific nor abrogated", and *Wikipedia*, citing Jonathan Brown (*Misquoting Muhammad*, p. 186), calls it as absolute and universal a statement as one finds ({hadith:abudawud:2682} for the occasion; al-Albani: *ṣaḥīḥ*). Classical law also had *ḥisba*, the duty to enjoin right and forbid wrong; how far it was used to enforce dress has not yet been checked. The modern argument, made by Dar al-Iftaʾ in its fatwa, is practical and moral as well as textual: a father "must, to the best of his ability, persuade his daughter", "must refrain from beating or harming her", and must keep supporting her, because "any compulsion will lead her to be hypocritical of religion and insincere". Worship done under force is not what the obligation asks for. *Limit:* 2:256 is about conversion; applying it to enforcement among Muslims is an extension, supported by the verse's general wording and by Dar al-Iftaʾ's reasoning, but not the only classical position.

**Iran.** In 1979 Khomeini said women should observe Islamic dress; hijab became mandatory in public offices in 1980 and for all women in 1983, with imprisonment of ten days to two months or fines under Penal Code article 638. In September 2022 Mahsa Amini died in the custody of Iran's morality police, three days after her arrest; a UN fact-finding mission found that she "was subjected to physical violence that led to her death" and that "the State bears responsibility for her unlawful death" (A/HRC/55/67, 2024). Her death set off nationwide protests.

Q8.section: heart — For the heart and mind
Q8.paragraph: **You are not alone, and you are not uniquely bad.** In a study of 777 university students at 15 sites in 13 countries on six continents, 93.6% reported at least one unwanted intrusive thought in the previous three months (Radomsky et al., 2014). The study was of students, not of "the human population", but the finding is clear: such thoughts are nearly universal. What differs is how much they stick.

Q15.paragraph: **Three ways every du'a is answered.** Abu Saʿid al-Khudri (ra) reports the Prophet (pbuh) as saying that no Muslim calls on God, without sin or cutting family ties, except that God gives him one of three: "He will quickly fulfill his supplication", "He will store it for him in the Hereafter", or "He will divert an evil from him similar to it". The Companions said: "In that case we will ask for more." He replied: "Allah has even more" (Musnad Ahmad 11133, from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri; its chain graded good, *jayyid*, in the Darussalam edition. Al-Tirmidhi 3573, from ʿUbada ibn al-Samit, is a partial parallel with two outcomes — granting, or turning away a similar harm — graded *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ gharīb* by al-Tirmidhi).

**Du'a and salah.** *Salah* is the ritual prayer, five times a day, with set words and movements. *Du'a* is calling on God in your own words, at any time, for anything. The Prophet (pbuh) said: "Supplication is worship" ({hadith:tirmidhi:2969}; al-Tirmidhi: *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*; al-Albani: *ṣaḥīḥ*). Its point is that calling on God is itself an act of worship, whatever the outcome.

Q16.paragraph: **"Tie your camel".** A man asked whether to tie his camel and trust God or leave it loose and trust God; the Prophet (pbuh) said: "Tie it and rely (upon Allah)" (al-Tirmidhi 2517, narrated by Anas). Its grading is disputed: al-Tirmidhi called it *gharīb* (known through one route), Yahya al-Qattan is reported to have called it *munkar* (rejected), and modern graders called it acceptable: Zubayr ʿAli Zaʾi called it good (hadithunlocked.com), and al-Albani graded it *ḥasan* (*Takhrīj al-Mishkāt*). It should not be relied on alone; the principle it expresses — take precautions and trust God — is supported by the scholars below.

M3.paragraph: **Marriage and career.** Readers ask whether a parent can choose their spouse or career. The source read does not address these directly, and the other schools' positions have not yet been consulted. On marriage, the page "Does Islam treat women unequally?" discusses whose consent is required.

M5.section: scholars — How scholars have understood it
M5.paragraph: **Al-Ghazali's book on patience and gratitude.** Book 32 of al-Ghazali's *Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn* is devoted to the two; its first part explains patience and why it is "considered to be half of faith", and its second explains gratitude (publisher's description of Littlejohn's translation). The Companion ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud said: "Patience is half of faith" (al-Hakim, *al-Mustadrak*; al-Dhahabi: sound); these are his words, not the Prophet's (pbuh). The popular form "faith is half patience and half gratitude" was not found with a sound chain.

**Is "faith is half patience and half gratitude" a hadith?** Not in that form: no sound chain was found for it. The Companion ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud said "Patience is half of faith" (al-Hakim; al-Dhahabi: sound), as his own words, and al-Ghazali builds Book 32 on the idea.

M8.paragraph: In 27 experiments with 4,045 people, acts of kindness raised the doer's own well-being by a small-to-medium amount (δ = 0.28) (Curry et al., 2018). People who were randomly asked to spend money on others were happier than those asked to spend it on themselves (Dunn, Aknin & Norton, *Science*, 2008).

M9.paragraph: **Do not betray even the betrayer.** "Pay the deposit to him who deposited it with you, and do not betray him who betrayed you" ({hadith:abudawud:3535}; al-Albani: *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*; al-Tirmidhi: *ḥasan gharīb*; al-Bayhaqi judged its chain weak).
The grade of "do not betray those who betrayed you" has not yet been checked. Cross-country trust research is correlational. Corruption scores for Muslim-majority countries have not yet been checked.

M10.paragraph: Al-Qurtubi (d. 1273, Córdoba and Egypt), commenting on 4:36, explains "the neighbor farther away" (*al-jār al-junub*) as "the stranger", following Ibn ʿAbbas, and reports the early view of Nawf al-Shami that it means a Jewish or Christian neighbour. His own judgement: care for the neighbour is "commanded and recommended, whether the neighbour is a Muslim or a non-believer — and that is the correct view." He cites a hadith of three kinds of neighbour, in which the neighbour with one right "is the unbeliever: he has the right of neighbourhood". He also reports, without giving its chain, the saying "Forty houses are neighbours", and that al-Awzaʿi and Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri counted "forty houses in every direction". Ibn Kathir gives the three-neighbours hadith from al-Bazzar, through Jabir; its grade has not yet been checked, so nothing rests on it.

M12.section: scholars — The hardest critique: Lynn White
M12.paragraph: Early commentators read *khalīfa* (2:30, "a successive authority") as humankind succeeding earlier beings on earth; al-Tabari explains it as one who "replaces the one who was before him"; later, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi read it as God's deputy who carries out His law (Liew, *Arabica*, 2016).

M13.paragraph: **What rights do spouses have in Islamic law?** Not covered in detail here; the page "Does Islam treat women unequally?" discusses the main rights and duties.

M14.paragraph: **"Seeking knowledge is a duty upon every Muslim."** This often-quoted saying is in Sunan Ibn Majah 224, narrated by Anas (ra): "Seeking knowledge is a duty upon every Muslim, and he who imparts knowledge to those who do not deserve it…" — the rest compares that to putting jewels on swine. Its grade is disputed: al-Albani accepted this first sentence as *ṣaḥīḥ* through its many routes, while al-Bayhaqi said its "text is well known and its chains are weak", and Zubayr ʿAli Zaʾi grades it weak. The second half of the same report is very weak by all accounts. Under this site's rules, no claim rests on it alone. The duty to learn what one needs for faith and practice is supported by the scholars below.

M15.paragraph: **The self that urges evil (12:53).** "And I do not acquit myself. Indeed, the soul is a persistent enjoiner of evil, except those upon which my Lord has mercy" (12:53). Ibn Kathir holds that the speaker is the minister's wife, admitting her fault before the king — "the most viable" reading of the story — while al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim report it as Joseph's words. Either way, the sentence is a confession that the self pulls towards wrong.

Q27.paragraph: **What is complicated about it.** The Persians took Jerusalem in 614; Heraclius defeated them near Nineveh on "Saturday, 12 December", as the Byzantine chronicler Theophanes records (trans. Mango & Scott, 1997) — in 627 by modern reckoning; the war ended in 628. The Ibn Kathir page read does not give dates. Second, an old variant reading vowels the verbs the other way — the Byzantines "have overcome… and will be defeated" — reported in the tafsir literature; the Ibn Kathir page read here does not mention it, so it is noted as unverified. A fair reader will say: the prediction was made in Mecca, at a time when Rome looked beaten; it came true; and the reports about it come from Muslim sources.

Q4.paragraph: **The Birmingham leaves.** The University of Oxford's Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit dated the parchment to 1456 ± 21 years before 1950, which corresponds, with 95.4% probability, to the years 568–645 CE (University of Birmingham, Cadbury Research Library). The date is the parchment's, not the writing's. *BP* means "before present", where "present" is fixed at 1950. The range begins before the Quran's revelation began — which shows the limits of the method: radiocarbon dates the death of the animal whose skin became the parchment, not the writing. David Thomas notes the text "could have been written as late as 650–655"; François Déroche has "expressed reservations about the reliability of the radiocarbon dates" (*Wikipedia*).

**The Sanaa palimpsest.** A *palimpsest* is a manuscript whose first text was scraped off and written over. In the Sanaa manuscript, both layers are Quran. Sadeghi and Bergmann found "a 95% probability that the parchment was produced… between 578 and 669 CE", and a 91.8% probability that it is older than 655.5 CE (as summarised by Nicolai Sinai, *BSOAS*, 2014). The lower text "contains many variations from the standard text", and its sura order "corresponds to no known Quranic order". Two examples: at 2:196, where the standard text has *fa-man kāna minkum* ("whoever among you"), the lower text has *fa-in kāna aḥadun minkum* ("if one of you"); at 9:125, where the standard text has "in their hearts is *disease*" (*maraḍ*), the lower text has "in their hearts is *filth*" (*rijs*). *Wikipedia*'s own judgement, without a citation, is that the variants "rarely diverge from the fundamental meaning". It also cites Éléonore Cellard as finding "numerous similarities" with the sura orders reported for Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy. Sadeghi and Goudarzi find some overlap with Ibn Masʿud's reported variants but "the differences much outnumbering the correspondences"; Asma Hilali argues both layers may be "school exercises", a view Nicolai Sinai has criticised.

Q11.paragraph: **A worked example of grading.** The hadith "Tie it and rely (upon Allah)", discussed on the page on earthquakes and disasters, (al-Tirmidhi 2517) was called *gharīb* by al-Tirmidhi: he knew it from Anas only by this one route, and he noted a similar report from ʿAmr b. Umayya al-Damri. Yahya al-Qattan called it *munkar* (rejected); Zubair ʿAli Zaʾi graded it *ḥasan* (good); and Ibn Hibban (no. 731) has a version graded *ḥasan li-ghayrihi* ("good because of support from other routes") by al-Arnaʾut. So a familiar saying can rest on a disputed chain. By contrast, the three-outcomes hadith on du'a (Musnad Ahmad 11133) has a chain al-Arnaʾut called *jayyid* (good), al-Hakim authenticated, and a parallel in al-Adab al-Mufrad (no. 710; *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Adab al-Mufrad* 547) graded *ṣaḥīḥ* by al-Albani. Grading is done chain by chain, and agreement between independent chains strengthens a report.

Q12.paragraph: The astrophysicist Nidhal Guessoum gives a detailed critique of the "scientific miracles" literature in *Islam's Quantum Question* (2011), as described by Hawramani's review.

S1.paragraph:
- **A seed is dormant, not dead.** [Established] A dry seed looks lifeless but is alive: as the next points show, it can wait for years and still grow when water reaches it.
- **Splitting begins with water.** [Established] UF/IFAS describes three phases. "Early seed germination begins with imbibition of water": the dry seed soaks up water and swells. Then comes "a period where there is little water uptake called the lag phase". Finally "water uptake drives the emergence of the radicle": the embryonic root breaks through the seed coat.
- **The hard date stone.** [Established] (2005): the date's stored food is a carbohydrate (galactomannan) laid down in very thick cell walls, which is why the stone is so hard; it is broken down mainly after the root has emerged. (This study has not yet been consulted again.)
- **How long a seed can wait.** [Established for the one seed; Moderate for the general point] A date seed excavated at Masada in the 1960s, then stored at room temperature for about four decades, was planted in 2005 by a team led by Sarah Sallon (Hadassah Medical Organisation), and cared for by Elaine Solowey. Fragments of its own shell were radiocarbon-dated to about 2,000 years old, "give or take about 50 years" (National Geographic, reporting Sallon et al., *Science*, 2008). Sallon put its survival down to Masada's hot, dry climate, which limited damage from free radicals, "a major force in seed ageing".
- **Not a single freak.** By 2020, seven ancient date seeds from three sites in the Judean desert, between about 1,800 and 2,400 years old, had sprouted. Thirty-five seeds had been planted in all (Sallon et al., *Science Advances*, 2020; Gros-Balthazard et al., *PNAS*, 2021). The paper itself was not opened.

S4.paragraph:
- **The popular claim.** The best-known form is Keith Moore's: a Canadian anatomist who, by his own account, worked with an embryology committee at King Abdulaziz University and produced an edition of his textbook *The Developing Human* "with Islamic Additions" (1982/83). He is quoted as saying the Quran's descriptions "cannot be based on scientific knowledge in the seventh century" (Islamic Awareness). Photo captions there describe his "Investigations in to the *'alaqa* or leech-like stage".
- **Weighing it.**
  - The words *ʿalaqa* and *muḍgha* fit the appearance of the embryo strikingly well, and that is worth noticing.
  - But the commentators read here take *ʿalaqa* as a blood clot (Ibn Kathir; ʿIkrima: "This is blood"; al-Jalālayn), not as a leech. The leech reading was not found in the classical sources read.
  - "We made [from] the lump, bones, and We covered the bones with flesh" can be read as a strict sequence: bones first, then muscle. Modern embryology shows the cartilage skeleton and muscle developing in the same weeks, overlapping (Lecturio; LifeMap). A possible reply (this page's own, not from a named source) is that "covered" describes the muscles wrapping the skeleton, not that they start later. Both readings are possible; neither is proven by the text.
  - The fair position: the verses can be read in harmony with embryology at a general level; they are not a textbook, and the commentators read here did not read them as one.
- **The forty-day hadith.** {hadith:bukhari:3208} speaks of forty-day stages. How its timings relate to modern embryology is disputed among Muslim scholars; that debate has not yet been consulted in a named source.
- The historian of science Joseph Needham, quoting the Quran's embryological verses, described them as "A seventh-century echo of Aristotle" (*A History of Embryology*, 1959) — a judgement this page weighs in its notes on 23:14.

S5.paragraph:
**How scholars read the prostration.** They differ, and the differences are worth stating:
- **Al-Khattabi**, *Aʿlām al-Ḥadīth* (commentary on al-Bukhari): "It cannot be denied that it halts beneath the Throne, in a manner that we cannot see or comprehend" (IslamQA's translation). For him the manner belongs to the unseen.
- **Ibn Hajar**, *Fatḥ al-Bārī*, offers several readings without insisting on one: it may be "the prostration of the angel charged with it", or the sun "prostrates by the state it is in", that is, by its submission. He reports Ibn al-ʿArabi: "Some people denied its prostration, though it is sound and possible" (quoted in Ibn Hajar, *Fatḥ al-Bārī* 6/299), while others read it as the sun's permanent state of subjection (SeekersGuidance's renderings).
- ***Maʿārif al-Qurʾān*** calls the prostration "simply a similitude in consonance with the mores of effective prophetic teaching": the sun "is nowhere but under the ʿArsh, at all times and at every place", so it "at every moment while moving on its orbit keeps offering sajdah" and "needs no pause or break".
- **Ibn Kathir** (in *al-Bidāya wa al-Nihāya*, cited by SeekersGuidance through al-Qastallani) holds that "nothing in this hadith says the sun ascends above the heavens to prostrate": it sets from our sight while continuing in its orbit.

Each point is tied to a phrase in the verses.
- **"We have determined for it phases" (36:39).** The Moon circles the Earth relative to the stars in 27.32 days, but new moon to new moon takes 29.53 days, because the Earth has moved along its own orbit in the meantime (NASA Moon Fact Sheet). So the Moon needs just over two more days to line up with the Sun again. Phases depend on the Sun–Earth–Moon angle, so a full cycle of phases, new moon to new moon, is the 29.5-day month. That is the length of a lunar (Islamic) month: 29 or 30 days.
- **"Until it returns [appearing] like the old date stalk" (36:39).** [Established] Before and after new moon, only a thin curved edge of the lit half faces us: the crescent the verse compares to a dried date stalk.
- **"The sun runs" (36:38).** [Established] The Sun is not fixed. It carries the solar system around the centre of our galaxy at an average speed of about "230 km/s (828,000 km/h)" (*Wikipedia*, "Galactic year", citing NASA StarChild, February 2000). Radio measurements put the Sun about 8.3 kiloparsecs (some 27,000 light-years) from the centre of the galaxy, moving at about 240 km/s (Reid et al., *Astrophysical Journal*, 2014). At that speed one circuit takes a little over 200 million years.
- **"Nor does the night overtake the day" (36:40).** [Established] Day and night follow each other as the Earth turns; at every moment it is day on one half of the Earth and night on the other.
- **The skeptic's point about the hadith.** [Established] Because of the same rotation, the Sun is always setting somewhere and rising somewhere else. (What this means for the hadith of the sun's prostration is discussed in "Honest notes", not here.)

S7.paragraph: Sura al-Raḥmān is Meccan in the view of most commentators, though some (al-Zamakhshari, al-Suyuti) place it in Medina (as summarised by *Wikipedia*). The verses that follow say pearls and coral come from both (55:22, paraphrased here; not quoted from verified data), and each sign in the sura is followed by a refrain asking which of the Lord's favours the listeners would deny (55:13 and after, paraphrased).

Each point is tied to the verses' words "released… meeting", "fresh and sweet… salty and bitter" and "barrier".
- **Where fresh meets salt.** [Established] In an estuary, where a river meets the sea, fresh water "floats on top of the heavier seawater" because it is less dense (NOAA). This is the nearest physical picture of 25:53: "one fresh and sweet and one salty and bitter", side by side.
- **How sharp the boundary is depends on tides and river flow.** [Established] NOAA classifies estuaries by how much they mix:
  - "Salt-wedge estuaries occur when a rapidly flowing river discharges into the ocean where tidal currents are weak": a sharp boundary, fresh above, a wedge of salt below.
  - In partially mixed estuaries "saltwater and freshwater mix at all depths", but the lower layers stay saltier.
  - In well-mixed estuaries, "Strong tidal currents eliminate the vertical layering".
  So a "barrier" of density can be sharp, gradual or absent.
- **Two salt seas: Gibraltar.** [Established] Mediterranean water leaving through the Strait of Gibraltar has a salinity of "38 g/kg" and a temperature of "13 °C", "extremely high compared with any other waters in that depth range". It exits at about 120 m depth and sinks to an equilibrium depth of about 1,100 m, at a rate of about 1 Sverdrup (a million cubic metres per second) (*Wikipedia*, "Mediterranean outflow").
- **But it does mix.** At Gibraltar, tides flowing over the Camarinal Sill create "an internal bore", which breaks into internal waves that drive strong mixing (*Wikipedia*). As it leaves Gibraltar, the Mediterranean water (salinity about 38.6) mixes so strongly with Atlantic water that by the time it settles, at around 900–1,000 m, its salinity has fallen to about 36.5 (Price & Yang, WHOI; Sánchez-Román et al., 2018). Mediterranean water also leaves in spinning lenses called *meddies*, typically 40–150 km across and about 800 m thick. At least 17 form each year, and some last four or five years and travel well over a thousand kilometres (Richardson, Bower & Zenk, *Progress in Oceanography*, 2000).
- **The viral video.** [Established] A widely shared photo said to show "two oceans meeting but not mixing" in the Gulf of Alaska shows, according to Lead Stories, "another river plume taken during a research cruise in the Gulf of Alaska" (photo by Kent Smith, 2010). Ocean Networks Canada, quoted there, describes a similar plume as "a puddle of light water (formed by mixing fresh Fraser water with salt water)".

Q2.paragraph: The creed of al-Tahawi (d. 933), a short statement of Sunni belief, says: "The exact nature of the decree is Allah's secret in His creation", and warns against "delving into it" too far (art. 45).

**What Libet found.** In Benjamin Libet's 1983 experiments, people flexed a wrist whenever they liked and reported, by a clock, when they first felt the urge. In Libet's 1983 study, when people moved on a sudden urge, the brain signal began on average about 350 milliseconds before the moment they reported first feeling the urge (Libet et al., *Brain*, 1983). Many took this to show that the brain "decides" before we do. Libet himself proposed that consciousness can still veto an action ("free won't").

**Why later work does not take it to settle free will.** [Moderate]
- Schurger, Sitt and Dehaene (2012) proposed that when the drive to move is weak, "the precise moment at which the decision threshold is crossed […] is largely determined by spontaneous subthreshold fluctuations in neuronal activity"; averaging many trials makes these fluctuations look like a gradual build-up. On this view, the readiness potential may not be a hidden decision at all.
- A 2019 study found the readiness potential for arbitrary choices but found it "strikingly absent" for deliberate, meaningful choices (Maoz et al., *eLife*, 2019, with 18 participants). Libet-style results may not apply to the choices that matter morally.
- Daniel Dennett and others questioned the timing method itself, which relies on people's reports of when they noticed an urge (*Wikipedia*).
- Above all, the task — flexing a wrist at a random moment, with nothing at stake — is very different from the moral choices religion is about.

Q5.section: quran — What the Quran says about Adam's creation
Q5.paragraph: **Adam like Jesus (3:59).** "Indeed, the example of Jesus to Allah is like that of Adam. The verse came, according to Ibn Ishaq as reported by Ibn Kathir, when a Christian delegation from Najran argued in Medina that Jesus (pbuh) was divine; its point is that Adam, created "without a father or a mother", is the greater wonder. It answers a question about Jesus; it was not given to settle biology. The comparison is that both came into being in an unusual way, by God's command.

**Common descent.** [Established] One clear example: humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, while "all other extant members of Hominidae have twenty-four pairs". In 1991 Ijdo and colleagues found, in the middle of human chromosome 2, two sets of telomere sequence (which normally sit only at chromosome ends) facing each other — "the relic of an ancient telomere-telomere fusion" that "marks the point at which two ancestral ape chromosomes fused" (*PNAS*, 1991). (Credit the "second centromere" to *Wikipedia* or to a source that reports it.) Chimpanzees have "nearly identical DNA sequences to human chromosome 2, but they are found in two separate chromosomes". This is one line of evidence among many (fossils, anatomy, shared genetic "mistakes"), which this page does not survey.

Q17.section: science — What cosmology does and does not show
Q17.paragraph: **The Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem (2003).** Borde, Guth and Vilenkin (2003) showed that a universe that has on average been expanding "must be incomplete in null and timelike past directions" — in plain words, its history cannot be followed back forever. Their argument needs no assumption about the kind of energy in the universe. Some later physicists dispute how far the result reaches (e.g. *Physical Review D* 107:044024, 2023). [Established, within its assumptions]

Q17.section: science — What cosmology does and does not show
Q17.paragraph: **The quantum-causation challenge.** Critics such as Paul Davies doubt that cause and effect can be defined consistently in fundamental physics; Quentin Smith cites virtual particles as uncaused; Lawrence Krauss proposes that quantum fluctuations could produce a universe. William Lane Craig replies that such events still have "many physically necessary conditions" (*Wikipedia*, "Kalam cosmological argument"). *Limit:* this debate is unresolved; and Vilenkin himself, in a 2015 essay, asked "What causes the universe to pop out of nothing?" and answered "No cause is needed" ("The Beginning of the Universe", *Inference*, 2015, as quoted by Craig).

Q30.section: quran — The Quran's arguments for resurrection
Q30.paragraph: The Quran promises that believers will be joined by their believing descendants (52:21), and that the righteous among their "fathers, their spouses and their descendants" will enter the Gardens with them (13:23; also the angels' prayer in 40:8). The condition is stated: righteousness, or following "in faith".

**Al-Ghazali: bodily resurrection.** In the conclusion of *The Incoherence of the Philosophers*, al-Ghazali names three theses that make the philosophers unbelievers; one is "their denial of the resurrection of bodies" (trans. Kamali). His target was above all Ibn Sina. In the *Tahāfut*, to refute the philosophers on their own premises, he argued that even if the soul survives, God could return it to a body, "ister bu beden insan bedeninin aynısı isterse de gayrısı olsun" — whether the same human body or another. But in *al-Iqtiṣād fī al-iʿtiqād* he says that this concession "bizim inancımıza uygun değildir" — "is not in accordance with our belief" — because that book was written to refute, not to prove (Yılmaz's Turkish rendering). Yılmaz judges that al-Ghazali stayed deliberately ambiguous about the soul's nature. For him, bodily resurrection is a matter "vahiyle vurgulanmış ve gerçekleşmesi imkânsız olmayan" — stressed by revelation and not impossible (Yılmaz). His point against the philosophers was that they had not *proved* it impossible.

S9.paragraph:
- **The popular claim.** Fine-tuning is often presented as proof that God exists, and 25:2 or 54:49 as having foretold it. Neither is warranted. The verses speak of measure and decree; the commentators read them as about God's decree (Ibn Kathir reports that the Imams of the Sunnah used 54:49 against the Qadariyya), not about physical constants.
- **The science is real; the inference is debated.** That some constants are life-permitting only in narrow ranges is widely accepted. Whether this points to design, a multiverse or a deeper law is a philosophical question, and the probability calculations behind each are disputed (SEP).
- The physicist Steven Weinberg, examining the famous carbon-12 case, concluded that "the fine-tuning of the constants of nature here does not seem so fine" — while granting that the cosmological constant "does seem remarkably well adjusted in our favor" (*New York Review of Books*, 1999).

Q37.section: scholars — Are deeds part of faith? The classical debate
Q37.paragraph: **Why it mattered.** In the first Islamic century, the Kharijites held that a person who commits a grave sin leaves Islam (*Wikipedia*, "Murji'ah"). The Kharijites held "that serious sinners should be ousted from the community"; the Murjiʾa answered that "no one who once professed Islam could be declared kāfir (infidel), mortal sins notwithstanding", and left judgment to God (*Britannica*, "Murjiʾah"). The later schools took positions between these.

Q10.paragraph: **Prayer times.** The Quran names times of prayer in several verses: "And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night" (11:114); "Establish prayer at the decline of the sun [from its meridian] until the darkness of the night and [also] the Qur'an of dawn" (17:78); see also 30:17–18. It does not state the number five.

Q10.section: scholars — Ibn al-Qayyim's five grades of people in prayer
Q10.paragraph: Al-Ghazali sums up the inner life of prayer "in six words": awareness (presence of the heart), understanding, reverence, awe, hope and shame (*Iḥyāʾ*, Book 4, *Asrār al-Ṣalāt*, trans. Zidan).

No technique guarantees feeling. Al-Qushayri's own text and any study of prayer's physiological effects have not yet been consulted. The practical steps beyond Rabbani's are general teaching, not sourced here.

Q9.section: scholars — How the commentators read "to worship Me"
Q9.paragraph: **Ibn Kathir.** "I, Allah, only created them so that I order them to worship Me, not that I need them." He reports Ibn ʿAbbas: "So that they worship Me, willingly or unwillingly." He also cites a hadith in which God says: "O Son of Adam! "O son of Adam! Devote yourself to My worship, I will fill your chest with riches and alleviate your poverty" ({hadith:tirmidhi:2466}; al-Tirmidhi: *ḥasan gharīb*; al-Albani: *ṣaḥīḥ*).

Q18.paragraph: The Prophet (pbuh) said that religion is sincere good will (*naṣīḥa*): "For Allah, His Book, His Messenger and for the leaders and the general Muslims" ({hadith:muslim:55}). Sincere counsel to leaders is part of the religion, not disloyalty to it.

**The 2016 coup attempt.** In 2017 the UK House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee reportedly accepted that some Gülenists were involved, but found that the claim that the movement as a whole and its leadership were behind the coup "is not substantiated by hard, publicly available evidence" (as reported by Al Jazeera, 25 March 2017). About 300 people were killed. President Erdoğan said the plotters were "linked to the Gülen movement", which the government later designated "FETÖ". Fethullah Gülen said: "I categorically deny such accusations." Germany's intelligence chief said Germany was unconvinced, and a British parliamentary committee found "no hard evidence that Fethullah Gülen masterminded the failed coup", though some Gülenists were involved. In the aftermath, "150,000 government officials and workers" were suspended (*Wikipedia*). This page takes no side in Turkish party politics. Whether, and how much, these events damaged young people's trust in religion is a question for survey data, and none was read.

Q19.section: sunnah — The 73-sects hadith, and the reward for honest error
Q19.paragraph: Ibn Taymiyya (d. 1328) rejected reading the hadith as a verdict of unbelief on the 72: the claim that all the sects are unbelievers, he wrote, "was only said by some later scholars", while the early generations and the imams did not declare the Murjiʾa or the Shiʿa unbelievers (*Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā* 3/351). S. S. Abdallah summarises his position: "He warns against summary excommunication of any Muslim groups, as long as they still profess the teachings of Islam" (*Afkar*, 2006).

Q19.section: sunnah — The 73-sects hadith, and the reward for honest error
Q19.paragraph: He did not excuse everyone: some innovators, he wrote, are hidden heretics and so unbelievers, but others "have strong Iman" and "are neither hypocrites nor infidels" (trans. Abdallah, 2006).

Q19.section: sunnah — The 73-sects hadith, and the reward for honest error
Q19.paragraph: Al-Baghdadi (d. 1037) built his *al-Farq bayna al-firaq*, the main source for later books on sects, around this hadith, starting from its first chapter (Abdallah, 2006).

**Earlier recognition.** In 1959 Mahmud Shaltut, rector of al-Azhar, issued a fatwa that the Jaʿfari (Shiʿi) school "is a school of thought that is religiously correct to follow in worship as are other Sunni schools of thought" (text as published by al-islam.org).

Q19.section: history — What the main groups believe and differ on
Q19.paragraph: **Ahmadis.** The Ahmadiyya were "founded by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad (1835–1908)" in British India; Ahmadis regard him as "divinely appointed as both the promised Messiah and Mahdi" and as a prophet without a new law — in Wikipedia's words, "a true reflection of Muhammad's prophethood". Mainstream Muslims regard this as heresy because they believe Muhammad (pbuh) was the "final prophet" (*khātam al-nabiyyīn*). In 1974 Pakistan amended its constitution so that anyone who does not accept that Muhammad (pbuh) is the final prophet "is not a Muslim for the purposes of the Constitution or law", naming the Ahmadis (Second Amendment, 1974, Arts. 106 and 260). The Amman Message does not list them; the pages read do not mention them or give a reason. Whatever one's view, it is a core-level dispute, not a difference of law.

Q19.section: reasoning — Is there a shared core?
Q19.paragraph: The saying "Disagreement in my community is a mercy" is not an established hadith: al-Sakhawi reported that "many imams held that it has no basis", and al-Bayhaqi cited it without a chain (as gathered by Rashid Rida).

Q19.section: objection — The strongest objections, and the replies
Q19.paragraph: **"Sunnis and Shiʿis killed each other for centuries."** *Reply:* yes, often when sectarian identity was fused with dynastic or state power (from Karbala to modern Iraq and Syria, per *Wikipedia*). Among the senior scholars whose rulings the Amman Message gathered was the Shiʿi authority Ayatollah Sistani (ammanmessage.com). *Limit:* recognition on paper has not ended conflict.

S26.paragraph:
- In 17 years of video surveys off California, from the surface to 3,900 m, 76% of the animals seen could make light, and the share was about the same at every depth (Martini & Haddock, *Scientific Reports*, 2017).
- Red is the first colour the sea takes away; by 100 m it is gone, and a red fish looks black (NOAA).
- In clear ocean the lit layer can reach about 200 m; in murky water, as little as 15 m (*Wikipedia*).

S27.paragraph: **A hadith Ibn Kathir cites.** Abu Hurayra (ra) reports that the Prophet (pbuh), on "some of them We make more excellent than others to eat", named kinds of dates: "The Daqal, the Persian …, the sweet, the bitter" ({hadith:tirmidhi:3118}). Al-Tirmidhi graded it *ḥasan gharīb*, and al-Albani *ḥasan*. Zubayr ʿAli Zaʾi graded it weak, because one narrator, al-Aʿmash, reports it with the vague "from" (*ʿan*) ({hadith:tirmidhi:3118}). Because its grade is disputed, nothing on this page rests on it.

- **No popular "miracle" claim was found** for this verse in the sources read. The risk here is the opposite: treating the verse as if it denied natural causes. It does not; it attributes the variety to God and asks people to reason about it.
- **Science and the verse.** The vineyard study shows that neighbouring soils differ, which fits the commentators' picture. It does not test the verse and should not be presented as confirming it.
- **Al-Rāzī.** That may well be so, but his commentary on 13:4 has not yet been consulted, so the claim cannot stay unsourced.
- **The hadith of the dates** (Tirmidhi 3118) has a disputed grade; it is reported, not relied on.
- Ibn Kathir calls the verse "among the greatest proofs of the Agent who chooses", and al-Qurtubi argues that if water, soil and nature alone were at work, plants watered with the same water would not differ. Al-Razi's commentary has not yet been consulted.

S30.paragraph:
Each point is tied to "gave each thing its form" and "destined" (a measure set in advance).
- **A written set of instructions.** [Established] DNA carries an organism's inherited instructions in four chemical "letters". "One complete set of genomic instructions is about 3 billion base pairs" (NHGRI, *Human Genome Project FAQ*).
- **The full text, finally read.** [Established] In 2022 the Telomere-to-Telomere Consortium published a "complete 3.055 billion-base pair sequence" of one human genome (T2T-CHM13). It filled "the remaining 8% of the genome", adding "nearly 200 million base pairs" (Nurk et al., *Science*).
- **Fewer genes than expected.** In 2004 the International Human Genome Sequencing Consortium confirmed 19,599 protein-coding genes and estimated 20,000–25,000 in all — far below the "about 100,000" most scientists had expected a decade earlier (NHGRI, 2004, on the consortium's *Nature* paper). Much of the rest of the genome helps control when and where genes are used.

- **The popular claim.** It is often said that DNA proves design. The best-known version is Stephen Meyer's *Signature in the Cell* (2009), which argues that "intelligent design is therefore the best explanation for the emergence of life on this planet", because chance and chemistry have not been shown able to produce the information in DNA and proteins (*Wikipedia* summary). [Debated]
- **The reply.** The chemist Stephen Fletcher replied in the *Times Literary Supplement* (December 2009) that "natural selection is a chemical as well as a biological process", so it could act before the first cells (as quoted in Meyer's reply). In the US, a federal district court ruled in *Kitzmiller v. Dover* (20 December 2005, Judge John E. In 2005 a US federal judge, John E. Jones III, ruled that "ID is not science and cannot be adjudged a valid, accepted scientific theory" (*Kitzmiller v. Dover*, p. 89). A court ruling settles a question of law, not of science. *Limit:* a court ruling on what may be taught in schools does not settle the philosophical question of whether information points to a mind.
- **A Muslim alternative.** Shoaib Ahmed Malik argues, using al-Ghazālī's framework, that "his ideas can be used to reach an alignment between Islam and Neo-Darwinian evolution" (*Islam and Evolution*, Routledge, 2021, abstract). On this view, belief in God does not depend on gaps in biology.
- **This page's position.** DNA is presented as a sign that invites wonder, not as proof, and not as something the verses predicted.
- Stretched out, the DNA in one human cell is about two metres long, folded into a nucleus about a thousandth of a millimetre across (Salk Institute, 2017). Copying is extremely accurate: in the bacterium *E. coli*, about one error per ten billion letters per copy (Fijalkowska et al., 2012).

S31.paragraph:
These are modern facts about balance in nature. They connect to the verses only by reflection; the verses' own subject is justice.
- **One predator, a whole coast.** [Established] Comparing "western Aleutian Islands with and without sea otter populations", Estes and Palmisano found that "Sea otters control herbivorous invertebrate populations", and that "Removal of sea otters causes increased herbivory and ultimately results in the destruction of macrophyte associations" (large seaweeds such as kelp) (*Science*, 1974). Ecologists call such animals "keystone" species.
- **Yellowstone, and why simple stories fail.** [Debated] After wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995, it was widely said they set off a "trophic cascade" (a chain of effects down the food web) that restored willows. A 2025 study by Ripple and colleagues reported a 1,500% rise in willow crown volume. In a formal reply, Daniel MacNulty (Utah State) and colleagues argued that this estimate "relies on circular reasoning", because "height was used both to compute and to predict volume", and that the data show a "more modest and spatially variable response". David Cooper (Colorado State): "there is no evidence that predator recovery caused a large or system-wide increase in willow growth". MacNulty: "Predator effects in Yellowstone are real but context-dependent". The release also notes Hobbs et al. A Yellowstone experiment lasting more than twenty years found that once heavy elk browsing had turned willow stands into grassland, the landscape "resisted returning to previous conditions once the carnivores were restored" (Hobbs, Cooper et al., *Ecological Monographs*, 2024). The debate continues.

S33.paragraph:
- The Morpho's blue is made by shape alone; fill the shape with alcohol instead of air and the blue turns greenish (KQED; Kuntzleman).
- Most animals cannot make blue pigment at all (KQED).
- Human skin colour follows sunlight closely: darker skin protects folate from ultraviolet light, lighter skin lets enough UV-B in to make vitamin D, and each population's colour is "a compromise" between the two (Jablonski & Chaplin, *Journal of Human Evolution*, 2000).
